Many of the questions asked about networks concern something that moves through them. An
infection passes from person to person along their contacts, a rumor or a new product spreads
through a social network, and a failure in a power grid or a supply chain travels from one
component to the next. Closely related are questions about how a network holds together when
parts of it are lost: when servers fail, when roads close, or when people are vaccinated and
so removed from the chains of transmission.

The two kinds of question share their mathematics. Whether an outbreak can become an epidemic is
decided by whether the contacts that actually transmit form a large connected cluster, and whether
a network survives a loss of nodes is decided by whether the surviving nodes do. Both are questions
of *percolation*, the theory of when random removals break a network apart. This page simulates
epidemics on networks, uses percolation to explain their thresholds, compares strategies for
immunization and for choosing influential spreaders, and measures the robustness of networks to
failures and attacks.

## Two networks

The structure of a network shapes everything that spreads on it, and the most important single
feature is the spread of its degrees. Two networks of the same size and density show this. The first
is grown by preferential attachment, in which new nodes link to well-connected ones, so that a few
nodes become hubs; the second is a random graph, in which every pair of nodes is equally likely to
be linked (see [Generating graphs](05-generators.qmd)):

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

n = 2000
hubs = ec.Graph(graph_name="hubs").add_pa_graph(n, m=2, seed=1)
flat = ec.Graph(graph_name="random").add_gnm_graph(n, hubs.count_edges(), seed=1)
networks = {"hubs": hubs, "random": flat}

pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "network": name,
            "edges": graph.count_edges(),
            "mean_degree": graph.get_node_df()["degree"].mean(),
            "max_degree": graph.get_node_df()["degree"].max(),
            "mean_squared_degree": (graph.get_node_df()["degree"] ** 2).mean(),
        }
        for name, graph in networks.items()
    ]
)
```

Both networks have 2,000 nodes, 3,997 edges, and a mean degree of 4. In the random graph, no node
has more than 12 neighbors, while the largest hub of the other network has 103. The mean of the
squared degrees, 45 against 20, measures this difference, and it is the quantity that the theory of
spreading turns on.

## Simulating an epidemic

The classic model of an epidemic is the SIR model, in which every person is *susceptible*,
*infected*, or *recovered*. Infected people pass the infection to each of their susceptible
contacts with some probability, and after a while recover, becoming immune. On a network, the
contacts are the edges. In the simplest discrete-time version, each infected node has a single
step in which to infect each susceptible neighbor, with probability `beta`, and then recovers. A
simulation needs only the neighbors of each node, from
[`get_neighbors()`](../reference/Graph.get_neighbors.qmd), and a random number generator:

```{python}
def simulate_sir(graph, source, beta, rng):
    neighbors = {node: graph.get_neighbors(node) for node in graph.get_node_df()["id"]}
    infected, recovered = {source}, set()
    curve = [1]
    while infected:
        new = {
            other
            for node in infected
            for other in neighbors[node]
            if other not in infected and other not in recovered and rng.random() < beta
        }
        recovered |= infected
        infected = new
        curve.append(len(infected))
    return curve
```

The function returns the *epidemic curve*: the number of infected nodes at each step, from the
first case until the infection dies out. The total number ever infected is the sum of the curve.
A single run on the network with hubs, from a randomly chosen first case and with a transmission
probability of 0.3:

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
source = int(rng.integers(1, n + 1))
curve = simulate_sir(hubs, source, 0.3, rng)
sum(curve), curve
```

The infection lingers at one or two cases for seven steps, then takes off, peaks at step 13 with 156
nodes infected at once, and burns out after 23 steps, having reached 918 nodes, almost half of the
network. Epidemics on networks are random, though, and a single run says little. Two hundred runs on
each network, each from a random first case, give a picture of the typical outbreak:

```{python}
rows = []
for name, graph in networks.items():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
    for run in range(200):
        curve = simulate_sir(graph, int(rng.integers(1, n + 1)), 0.3, rng)
        rows.append(
            {
                "network": name,
                "size": sum(curve),
                "peak_step": int(np.argmax(curve)),
                "duration": len(curve) - 1,
            }
        )
outbreaks = pl.DataFrame(rows)

outbreaks.group_by("network").agg(
    major=(pl.col("size") > 100).mean(),
    attack_rate=pl.col("size").filter(pl.col("size") > 100).mean() / n,
    peak_step=pl.col("peak_step").filter(pl.col("size") > 100).median(),
    duration=pl.col("duration").filter(pl.col("size") > 100).median(),
).sort("network")
```

Outbreaks fall into two kinds: most either die out after a handful of cases or grow into a *major
outbreak* that reaches a large share of the network, with little in between. The threshold of 100
cases separates the two. The table shows how often a major outbreak occurs, the *attack rate*, the
share of the network that a major outbreak infects, and the median step of its peak and its
duration.

The hubs make a large difference. On the network with hubs, a major outbreak is more likely, 42%
against 33% of first cases, and it reaches more of the network, 43% against 31%. It also peaks and
ends much sooner: once the infection reaches a hub, the hub passes it to dozens of others at once,
and the hubs, being linked to each other, carry it quickly across the whole network. On the random
graph, the infection advances slowly, from neighbor to neighbor, and takes more than twice as long
to run its course.

## Outbreaks as percolation

In this model, each edge gets a single chance to transmit, with probability `beta`, whatever
happens elsewhere. Whether an edge would transmit can therefore be decided in advance, for all the
edges at once, and the outbreak from a first case is then simply the set of nodes it can reach along
the transmitting edges. Keeping each edge with probability `beta` is *bond percolation*, which
[`edge_percolation()`](../reference/Graph.edge_percolation.qmd) performs. Its `q=` is the share of
edges to remove, so `q=1 - beta` keeps the share `beta`. The outbreak from a node is its connected
component in the result, from
[`node_connected_component()`](../reference/Graph.node_connected_component.qmd):

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
sizes = []
for run in range(200):
    transmitting = hubs.edge_percolation(q=0.7, seed=run)
    sizes.append(len(transmitting.node_connected_component(int(rng.integers(1, n + 1)))))

round(np.mean(sizes)), round(outbreaks.filter(pl.col("network") == "hubs")["size"].mean())
```

The mean outbreak size from percolation agrees with that of the simulation, up to the noise of 200
runs each. The equivalence explains why outbreaks are either small or large. A percolated network
has, at most, one large connected cluster, the *giant component*, and many small ones. A first case
in a small cluster produces a small outbreak, and a first case in the giant component infects all
of it. The size of the giant component is the attack rate of a major outbreak, and the share of the
nodes in it is the chance that one occurs, which is why the two columns of the simulation's table
were so close to each other.

The equivalence holds whenever each contact transmits independently with a fixed probability, the
*transmissibility* `T`. In a model in which infected nodes stay infectious for several steps, each
with transmission probability `beta`, the transmissibility is the chance of at least one
transmission over the whole infectious period, such as `1 - (1 - beta) ** 3` for three steps.

### The epidemic threshold

The giant component of a percolated network exists only when enough edges are kept, so an epidemic
is possible only when the transmissibility is above a *threshold*. For a network with random
wiring, the theory of percolation gives the threshold from the degrees alone:
`T_c = <k> / (<k²> - <k>)`, where `<k>` is the mean degree and `<k²>` the mean squared degree.
For the two networks:

```{python}
thresholds = {}
for name, graph in networks.items():
    degree = graph.get_node_df()["degree"]
    thresholds[name] = round(degree.mean() / ((degree**2).mean() - degree.mean()), 3)
thresholds
```

The random graph needs a transmissibility of 0.25 for an epidemic, while the network with hubs
needs less than 0.1. The larger the mean squared degree, the lower the threshold: a hub is both
very likely to be infected, since it has so many neighbors, and very likely to pass the infection
on. For networks whose degrees follow a power law with an exponent of 3 or less, such as many
social and technological networks, `<k²>` grows without limit as the network grows, and the
threshold falls toward zero, so that even a barely transmissible infection can spread.

The size of the giant component over a range of transmissibilities shows the threshold in action.
[`largest_component_size()`](../reference/Graph.largest_component_size.qmd) gives the size of the
largest component, averaged here over twenty percolated copies of each network:

```{python}
def attack_rate(graph, transmissibility, runs=20):
    sizes = [
        graph.edge_percolation(q=1 - transmissibility, seed=run).largest_component_size()
        for run in range(runs)
    ]
    return round(float(np.mean(sizes)) / n, 3)


pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {"T": t} | {name: attack_rate(graph, t) for name, graph in networks.items()}
        for t in [0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7]
    ]
)
```

The random graph has no epidemic below a transmissibility of about 0.25, and a sharp rise above
it. The network with hubs has a small giant component already at 0.15 and a gradual rise, with no
sharp threshold. At 0.4 and 0.5, the order reverses, and the random graph's epidemics are slightly
larger: the many nodes of the network with hubs that have only two contacts each are easily
missed. Hubs make epidemics easier to start, not necessarily larger, and at high transmissibility
both networks are almost entirely infected.

Other models have thresholds of their own. In the SIS model, in which recovered nodes become
susceptible again, as with many bacterial infections, the infection persists when the ratio of the
infection and recovery rates exceeds about `1 / λ`, where `λ` is the largest eigenvalue of the
adjacency matrix, which [Other libraries](28-other-libraries.qmd#sparse-matrices) computes with
SciPy. Hubs raise the largest eigenvalue, and lower the threshold, in the same way.

## Immunization

Vaccinating a node removes it from every chain of transmission, as if it had been deleted from the
network, so immunization is node percolation: the question is how few nodes need to be removed for
the giant component of transmitting contacts to vanish. The choice of whom to immunize matters as
much as the number. Three strategies with the same number of doses compare as follows:

- **Random** immunization picks nodes at random, which is what a campaign without information about
  the network does.
- **Targeted** immunization picks the nodes of highest degree, which requires knowing the whole
  network.
- **Acquaintance** immunization picks random nodes and immunizes a random *neighbor* of each. Since
  a node with many neighbors is named as a neighbor often, this finds hubs without knowledge of the
  network, only of a few contacts of each person asked.

Each strategy returns a list of node IDs, and the immunized network is the
[`subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.subgraph.qmd) of the remaining nodes. Its attack rate at a
transmissibility of 0.3 comes from percolation, as before, and is measured as a share of the
whole population:

```{python}
def immunize(graph, doses, strategy, rng):
    nodes = graph.get_node_df()
    ids = nodes["id"].to_list()
    if strategy == "random":
        return rng.choice(ids, doses, replace=False).tolist()
    if strategy == "targeted":
        return nodes.sort("degree", descending=True)["id"].head(doses).to_list()
    chosen = set()
    while len(chosen) < doses:
        contacts = graph.get_neighbors(int(rng.choice(ids)))
        if contacts:
            chosen.add(int(rng.choice(contacts)))
    return list(chosen)


rows = []
for name, graph in networks.items():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
    for share in [0.05, 0.1, 0.2]:
        row = {"network": name, "immunized": share}
        for strategy in ["random", "targeted", "acquaintance"]:
            immune = set(immunize(graph, int(share * n), strategy, rng))
            remaining = graph.subgraph([v for v in graph.get_node_df()["id"] if v not in immune])
            row[strategy] = attack_rate(remaining, 0.3)
        rows.append(row)
pl.DataFrame(rows)
```

Without immunization, an epidemic at this transmissibility reaches 43% of the network with hubs and
31% of the random graph. Random immunization helps only in proportion to the doses: immunizing a
tenth of the network with hubs at random lowers the attack rate only from 43% to 33%. Targeting the
hubs is far more effective. Immunizing the best-connected 5% all but eliminates the epidemic, since
the hubs are the bridges through which it reaches most of the network. Acquaintance immunization,
without any knowledge of the network's structure, comes close: with a tenth of the network
immunized, the epidemic shrinks to about 4%.

On the random graph, every strategy works less dramatically, since there are no hubs to find, but
targeting the nodes of highest degree is still the most effective. The lesson is general: the
nodes that make a network vulnerable to spreading are also the ones whose removal protects it.

## Influential spreaders

The reverse problem arises when spreading is wanted, as with information, a public-health message,
or a new product: which few nodes should be chosen as *seeds*, to reach as much of the network as
possible? The usual model is the *independent cascade*, the same model as the epidemic above: each
newly activated node has one chance to activate each of its neighbors, with probability `p`.

The obvious choice, the nodes of highest degree, has a flaw: hubs tend to sit close together, and
seeds in the same region reach the same nodes. Two methods take the overlap into account.
[`voterank()`](../reference/Graph.voterank.qmd), described in
[Centrality](13-centrality.qmd#spreaders), elects seeds one at a time and weakens the votes of each
winner's neighbors, so that later seeds lie elsewhere.
[`influence_maximization()`](../reference/Graph.influence_maximization.qmd) chooses seeds greedily,
simulating cascades to find, at each step, the node that adds the most to the expected spread of
the seeds already chosen. On the dolphin social network, with five seeds and an activation
probability of 0.2:

```{python}
dolphins = ec.dolphins()
dolphins.cmty_louvain()
nodes = dolphins.get_node_df()

seed_sets = {
    "degree": nodes.sort("degree", descending=True)["id"].head(5).to_list(),
    "voterank": dolphins.voterank(count=5),
    "greedy": [
        node
        for node, gain in dolphins.influence_maximization(
            5, probability=0.2, n_simulations=500, seed=1, return_dict=True
        )
    ],
}
seed_sets
```

`influence_maximization()` returns each chosen node with its *marginal gain*, the estimated number
of additional nodes it reaches, and its `n_simulations=` sets the number of simulated cascades for
each estimate. The greedy search runs about `k * n_nodes * n_simulations` cascades, so it takes a
fraction of a second on a network of this size but tens of seconds on one of a few thousand nodes.

To compare the seed sets fairly, each is evaluated on the same percolated copies of the network.
The spread of a set of seeds in one copy is the union of their components, and its mean over many
copies is the expected spread:

```{python}
def expected_spread(graph, seeds, p, runs=2000):
    total = 0
    for run in range(runs):
        transmitting = graph.edge_percolation(q=1 - p, seed=run)
        reached = set()
        for node in seeds:
            if node not in reached:
                reached |= transmitting.node_connected_component(node)
        total += len(reached)
    return round(total / runs, 1)


spreads = {name: expected_spread(dolphins, seeds, 0.2) for name, seeds in seed_sets.items()}

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
random_sets = [rng.choice(nodes["id"].to_list(), 5, replace=False).tolist() for _ in range(20)]
spreads["random"] = round(np.mean([expected_spread(dolphins, s, 0.2, 200) for s in random_sets]), 1)
spreads
```

`rng.choice()` returns NumPy integers, and `tolist()` turns them into the Python integers that
EdgeCase accepts as node IDs. The random baseline averages twenty random seed sets.

The five best-connected dolphins reach about 20 of the 62, fewer than five dolphins chosen at
random, which reach about 21. VoteRank and the greedy search both reach about 26, a quarter more
than the hubs. The reason is visible when the seeds are drawn on the network, colored by the
communities that [Louvain](../reference/Graph.cmty_louvain.qmd) finds:

```{python}
marks = {
    node: ("D" if node in seed_sets["degree"] else "")
    + ("V" if node in seed_sets["voterank"] else "")
    for node in nodes["id"]
}
dolphins.set_node_attrs("seed", marks)
dolphins.plot(color_by="cmty_louvain", palette="Set2", label_by="seed", seed=3)
```

Nodes labelled `D` are among the five of highest degree, nodes labelled `V` were chosen by VoteRank,
and nodes labelled `DV` by both. Three of the five hubs lie in the same community, in teal, and the
other two in the neighboring orange community, so their cascades overlap. VoteRank keeps two of the
hubs but places two of its seeds in the blue community at the lower right, which none of the hubs
belong to. Its seeds lie in three communities, and those of the greedy search in four. The greedy
search reaches a similar spread with different seeds on different runs, since many seed sets do
almost equally well; its result is an estimate, and different values of `seed=` can give different
choices. The best seeds also depend on `p`: at low probabilities cascades stay local and high degree
matters most, while at high probabilities the seeds' positions in different parts of the network
matter more.

For a single spreader rather than a set, the *coreness* of a node from
[`coreness()`](../reference/Graph.coreness.qmd), its depth in the k-core decomposition (see
[Structure](11-structure.qmd)), is a good predictor of its reach, often better than its degree,
since a hub on the periphery of a network spreads less than a node in its dense core.

## Robustness

[Connectivity](16-connectivity.qmd#robustness) introduced
[`network_robustness()`](../reference/Graph.network_robustness.qmd), which removes nodes one at a
time, in random order or in order of degree or betweenness, and records the share of the original
nodes that remain in the largest component. The whole curve can be summarized by its mean, the
*robustness index* `R` of Schneider and colleagues, which is the area under the curve. It is close
to 0.5 for a network that shrinks only as fast as its nodes are removed, and close to 0 for one that
falls apart after the first few removals:

```{python}
def robustness_index(graph, strategy):
    curve = graph.network_robustness(strategy=strategy, seed=1, return_dict=True)
    return round(float(np.mean([share for removed, share in curve])), 3)


strategies = ["random", "degree", "betweenness"]
pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {"network": name} | {strategy: robustness_index(graph, strategy) for strategy in strategies}
        for name, graph in networks.items()
    ]
)
```

Under random failure, the two networks are about equally robust. Under an attack on the
best-connected nodes, the network with hubs is more than twice as fragile as the random graph. The
removal order is fixed from the intact network, by degree or by betweenness computed once, as in
most studies of attacks; an attacker who recomputes the degrees after every removal does only
slightly more damage here.

### The threshold of random failure

The theory of percolation also predicts how much random failure a network survives. For a network
with random wiring, the giant component survives the removal of a share of nodes `f` as long as
`f < 1 - 1 / (κ - 1)`, where `κ = <k²> / <k>` is the ratio of the mean squared degree to the mean
degree. For the two networks:

```{python}
critical = {}
for name, graph in networks.items():
    degree = graph.get_node_df()["degree"]
    kappa = (degree**2).mean() / degree.mean()
    critical[name] = round(1 - 1 / (kappa - 1), 2)
critical
```

The random graph should break up when about three quarters of its nodes have failed, and the
network with hubs only when nine tenths have.
[`node_percolation()`](../reference/Graph.node_percolation.qmd) removes a share `q=` of the nodes
at random, which tests the prediction:

```{python}
def giant_share(graph, removed, runs=20):
    sizes = [
        graph.node_percolation(q=removed, seed=run).largest_component_size()
        for run in range(runs)
    ]
    return round(float(np.mean(sizes)) / n, 3)


pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {"removed": f} | {name: giant_share(graph, f) for name, graph in networks.items()}
        for f in [0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9]
    ]
)
```

The random graph's giant component has all but vanished at three quarters of its nodes removed,
holding under 3% of the network, as the prediction says. The network with hubs has no sharp
collapse: its giant component fades gradually, and some of it survives beyond the point where the
random graph has broken up. For networks whose degrees follow a power law, the theory predicts that
the threshold approaches 1 as the network grows, so that no amount of random failure breaks up a
large enough network. A network of 2,000 nodes is far from that limit, and the effect is modest, but
it is the same effect that makes the Internet robust to the failure of random routers, while its
hubs make it fragile to attack.

[`percolation_threshold_analysis()`](../reference/Graph.percolation_threshold_analysis.qmd) runs
the same sweep in a single call, averaging over `trials=` random removals at each of `steps=`
evenly spaced shares. It reports the largest component as a share of the *surviving* nodes rather
than of all of them, which shows how well the survivors hold together (see
[Connectivity](16-connectivity.qmd#robustness)).

### Robustness and spreading

Random edge failure is bond percolation, the same process that decides the size of an epidemic. A
network whose giant component survives the loss of most of its edges is also one in which an
infection with low transmissibility can still spread, and the threshold `T_c` computed above is also
the share of edges that must survive random failure for a giant component to remain. The two views
lead to one conclusion: the hubs of a heterogeneous network hold it together against random failure
and carry epidemics across it, and they are its weak point when they are attacked, or protected.

## Summary

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| Simulate an epidemic and its curve | an SIR loop over `get_neighbors()`, with a random number generator |
| Sizes of outbreaks without simulation | `edge_percolation(q=1 - T)` and `node_connected_component()` |
| Epidemic threshold and attack rate | `<k> / (<k²> - <k>)`, and `largest_component_size()` of percolated copies |
| Effect of immunization | `subgraph()` of the remaining nodes, then the attack rate |
| Choose a set of spreaders | `influence_maximization()`, `voterank()` |
| Rank single spreaders | `coreness()`, `degree`, `percolation_centrality()` |
| Robustness to failure and attack | `network_robustness(strategy=)`, with its mean as the index `R` |
| Random failure | `node_percolation()`, `edge_percolation()`, `percolation_threshold_analysis()` |
